place.en: The hidden realm · The stone chamber

setup.zh: 墙后面是一间石室，四个空坑，一边七拃；石台上一只玉匣，匣子里一撮土。银月拼着最后一点灵气，在你脚底画了一道符，便睡死了。墙缝里站着一个黄袍，笑眯眯的：「会自己长的土？」
setup.en: Behind the wall, a stone chamber: four empty pits, seven hand-spans a side; on the altar a jade box, and in the box a pinch of earth. Yinyue spends the last of her strength drawing a charm on your soles, and sleeps like the dead. In the crack of the wall stands a yellow robe, smiling: "Earth that grows by itself?"

recap.zh: 石室里一撮息壤。赤松观的邹青松追了你一路：火蛇、那面「金丹以下，无人能破」的盾；踏马的符一跳，你落在蛫背后，火蛇撞灭在龟壳上。银月两根狐毛破了他的盾，你自己结果了他。你吞下息壤，五门俱开，练气四层。
recap.en: A pinch of xirang in the stone chamber. Zou Qingsong of the Red Pine Abbey chased you the length of the realm: fire snakes, and a shield nothing short of a Golden Core can break. One leap on the Hoof-It Charm put you behind the gui, and the fire snakes died on its shell. Yinyue broke his shield with two hairs from her tail; you finished him yourself. You swallowed the xirang: all five doors open, layer four of Qi Refining.

zh: 一张石台，一只玉匣。「息壤。」
脚底两匹歪马：「……这不就是饭桶吐出来那张？」
en: A stone altar, a jade box. "Xirang."
Two crooked horses on his soles: "…Isn't that the one Rice Bucket spat out?"

story.zh:
墙后面，是一间石室，方方正正，四壁青石打磨得光溜溜的，照得出人影。没有灵草，没有法器，也没有前人的骸骨，干干净净，像是昨天才有人扫过。西北角贴着地，有一个半人高的黑洞，墙外那股风，便是一阵一阵往那洞里吸的。正中一张石台，台上一只玉匣。可小满一进门，最先看见的，却不是那只玉匣。石室的地上，离石台三步远的地方，有四个坑。

四个方方的坑，一边一个，排成一个四方，每个有碗口大，一尺来深，坑底磨得溜光，坑沿磨得发亮，一圈青苔，青得发黑。他爹教过他看蹄印：印子深，是那东西沉；印子磨得发亮，是那东西在这里站了很久很久。一样极沉极沉的东西，四条腿，把石头都站出了坑。然后，它走了。

小满蹲下来，张开手掌，拇指抵着一个坑的外沿，一拃一拃地量到另一个坑的外沿——猎户量蹄印，向来是这么量的。一拃，两拃，三拃……七拃。另外三边，边边都是七拃。他想起二试那个老执事讲的：一千个人下泗水捞鼎，没捞着。这间石室里的灵气厚得化不开，外头的却薄得像刷锅水；他站在四个空坑中间，头一回隐隐约约地觉得，这两件事，也许是一件事。

石室的四壁，走近了才看得出有刻痕，极浅，极细。东墙是水，浪头卷着浪头，水里漂着房子，漂着伸着手的人。南墙是一个人，背着一只筐，从筐里抓出什么往水里撒，撒过的地方，水底下冒出一块一块的地来；那人的腰是弯的，像背着一样极重极重的东西。西墙是九样东西，三排，一排三个，每一样都四四方方，底下四只脚，两只耳朵。北墙是空的，刻满了浅浅的格子，格子里什么都没有；最底下，贴着地，有一个很小的刻痕，刻得比别的都深，都新：一只狐狸，蜷着身子，尾巴绕着身子，跟他胸口那块木牌上的，一模一样。银月跳下他的肩膀，走到那只刻出来的狐狸跟前，低下头，拿鼻子碰了碰它，尾巴垂着，又跳回他肩上，一句话也没有说。

他走到石台前，打开了玉匣。匣子里，只有**一撮土**。黄褐色的，松松的，刚好铺满匣底，跟他家后院那块种不出东西的地里的土没什么两样。小满盯着看了半天，道：「……就这？」肩上的银月却一字一字地道：「[息壤]{注=xirang}。」她的声音在抖，尾巴尖上的毛一根一根全竖了起来，「会自己长的土。你给它一粒，它长出一撮；给它一撮，它长出一座山。当年——」她停住了，像是在很深的井里捞一样东西，捞了半天，只捞上来半桶。她盯着地上那四个空坑，没有再往下说；隔了一会儿，才回过头来，一双金色的眼睛亮得有些发潮：「……本王不知道它是好东西。本王只知道，你是漏勺。」她把头转回去，声音低得像是自言自语：「一个漏勺，夜夜在柴垛上坐到后半夜，漏一夜，接着坐。坐了一年。……本王看着烦。」小满想说句什么，想起的又是那个「谢」字——在蒙山的柴垛上欠下的，欠到今天，还没还上。

她的鼻子抽了两抽，往墙缝那边望了一眼，又转回来，道：「抬脚。」小满不明白，还是脱了草鞋，抬起一只脚来。她拿尾巴尖在他脚底板上描，描得很慢，尾巴尖一边描一边抖；描完这一只，又描那一只。描完了，她整个儿淡了一层，淡得他看得见她身子后头的石台。小满扳着脚底板看：一边一个，四条腿，一个脑袋，一条尾巴。他认得这东西：「……这不就是饭桶吐出来那张？」银月道：「踏云符。」小满道：「踏马的符。」银月尾巴上的毛炸了一炸，又塌了下去，连吵嘴的力气都没了：「……这一张，灵。只灵一回。一口气。别浪费。」话没说完，她已化作一缕银光，钻回了木牌。木牌凉了，凉得像井底的一块石头。

他合上玉匣，盘腿坐在石台跟前等她醒，等了一顿饭的工夫，又一顿饭的工夫。她没说这土拿来做什么，他便不动它。石室里静得听得见西北角那个黑洞里的风，一吸，一停。

「会自己长的土？」

墙缝里站着一个人，赭黄袍子，白净脸，笑眯眯的，右手托着那只赤铜葫芦。邹青松道：「好东西。坑边那圈青苔也是——鼎苔，只长在站过鼎的地方。灵草园底下有个小丫头，一张地图背得一字不差，背到『左崖，没人去』——我便来了。你翻乌龟那一炷香，我就在石台那头那堆碎石后头；那二十三下，我也替你数着；上头那六个，你粘得好，省了我的事。」他往小满肩上看了一眼，「还有那只狐狸。」小满的心往下一沉：一张地图背得一字不差的小丫头，外门只有一个。他想起潭边滚下来的那一粒石子——这一天，他第二回把一样活物当成了石头。邹青松道：「匣子放下，狐狸放下。人嘛——」他想了一想，像在算一笔很小的账，「长廊里那个胖子，你看见了。」

小满把玉匣揣进怀里，摘下了背上的弓。这一回，他没有想藏。
story.en:
Behind the wall was a stone chamber, square, its walls of bluestone polished smooth enough to show a reflection. No herbs, no magic tools, no bones of the old ones; clean, as if swept yesterday. In the northwest corner, at floor level, was a black hole half a man high; the wind from outside the wall was being drawn into it, gust by gust. In the middle a stone altar, and on it a jade box. But the first thing Xiaoman saw as he came in was not the box. On the floor, three steps from the altar, were four pits.

Four square pits, one at each corner of a square, each the size of a bowl's mouth, a foot deep, their bottoms worn glassy, their rims worn shiny, each ringed with moss so green it was nearly black. His father had taught him to read hoofprints: a deep print means a heavy beast; a shiny one means it stood there a long, long time. Something very, very heavy, on four legs, had worn pits in the stone. Then it left.

Xiaoman crouched, spread his hand, set his thumb on the outer rim of one pit and spanned his way to the outer rim of the next, hand over hand — the way a hunter measures a print. One span, two, three… seven. The other three sides: seven spans each. He remembered what the old steward had told at the second test: a thousand men went down into the Si to fish up a cauldron, and didn't get it. The qi in this chamber was too thick to melt, while outside it was thin as dishwater; standing among four empty pits, he felt dimly, for the first time, that the two things might be one thing.

The four walls, up close, bore carvings, very shallow, very fine. The east wall was water, wave rolling over wave, houses floating, people floating with arms outstretched. The south wall was a man with a basket on his back, scattering something from it into the water; wherever he scattered, land rose piece by piece from under the water; his back was bent, as if under a very, very heavy load. The west wall was nine things in three rows of three, each square, on four legs, with two ears. The north wall was blank, covered in shallow squares with nothing in them; at the very bottom, against the floor, was one very small carving, cut deeper and newer than all the rest: a fox, curled up, its tail wrapped round its body — exactly like the one on the token on his chest. Yinyue jumped down from his shoulder, went to the carved fox, lowered her head and touched it with her nose, her tail hanging, then jumped back onto his shoulder without a word.

He went to the altar and opened the jade box. In it was only **a pinch of earth**. Yellow-brown, loose, just covering the bottom, no different from the soil in his family's yard where nothing grows. Xiaoman stared at it a long time. "…That's it?" But Yinyue on his shoulder said, word by word: "Breathing soil." Her voice shook; the fur on her tail tip stood up hair by hair. "Earth that grows by itself. Give it one grain, it grows a pinch; give it a pinch, it grows a mountain. Back then —" She stopped, like someone fishing in a very deep well who fished a long time and brought up only half a bucket. She stared at the four empty pits on the floor and said no more; after a while she turned her head, her golden eyes bright and a little wet: "…I don't know if it's a good thing. I only know you're a skimmer." She turned away again, her voice low, as if talking to herself: "A skimmer, sitting on the woodpile every night till past midnight, leaking all night, sitting on. Sat a whole year. …It got on my nerves." Xiaoman wanted to say something, and what came to him was that word again, "thank you" — owed since the woodpile on Mount Meng, owed to this day and still not paid.

Her nose twitched twice; she glanced toward the crack in the wall and back. "Lift your foot." Xiaoman didn't understand, but he took off a straw sandal and lifted one foot. She traced on its sole with the tip of her tail, very slowly, the tail tip trembling as it went; when she'd done that one, she did the other. When she'd finished, she had faded a whole layer — so faint he could see the altar through her. Xiaoman twisted his foot round to look at the sole: one on each, four legs, a head, a tail. He knew it: "…Isn't that the one Rice Bucket spat out?" "A Cloud-Step Charm," said Yinyue. "A Hoof-It Charm," said Xiaoman. The fur on her tail bristled and fell flat again; she hadn't even the strength to bicker. "…This one works. Once. One breath. Don't waste it." Before she had finished she became a wisp of silver light and slipped back into the token. The token went cold, cold as a stone at the bottom of a well.

He closed the jade box and sat cross-legged before the altar waiting for her to wake — the time of one meal, then another. She hadn't said what the earth was for, so he left it alone. The chamber was so quiet he could hear the wind in the black hole in the northwest corner: a draw, a pause.

"Earth that grows by itself?"

In the crack of the wall stood a man: ochre robe, fair face, all smiles, the red-bronze gourd cupped in his right hand. "A fine thing," said Zou Qingsong. "And that moss round the pits — cauldron moss; it grows only where a cauldron once stood. Down by the herb garden there's a little girl who had a whole map by heart, word perfect, right down to 'Left cliff, nobody goes' — so here I am. That stick of incense you spent turning the turtle, I was behind that heap of rubble at the far end of the ledge; those twenty-three — I counted them for you; the six up there — nicely stuck, you saved me the trouble." He glanced at Xiaoman's shoulder. "And the fox." Xiaoman's heart sank: a little girl who knew a whole map word perfect — there was only one in the outer court. He remembered the pebble that had rolled down by the pool — for the second time that day he had taken a living thing for a stone. "Put the box down," said Zou Qingsong, "and the fox. As for you —" He thought a moment, as if working out a very small sum. "That fat one in the corridor. You saw."

Xiaoman tucked the jade box into his coat and took the bow from his back. This time he had no thought of hiding.

exits.means: stops hiding: the bow (《落雁三箭》, the first arrow), the chase down the wind shaft to the dry riverbed and back to the ledge; the Hoof-It Charm's leap behind the gui; Yinyue's two hairs break the shield; he finishes Zou Qingsong himself, then swallows the breathing soil
exits._doors: The page's moment after this exit (story.mjs node `doors`): the five doors open one by one, a seal and a line each, in ink — colour is for 银月's memories alone.

doors.zh: 第一扇，金。「铮」的一声——是爷爷那张弓的弦。
doors.en: The first, Metal. A twang — the string of Grandpa's bow.

doors.zh: 第二扇，木。吱吱呀呀，像黑松岭的松树，在没有风的夜里自己挪了一步。
doors.en: The second, Wood. Creak by creak, like the pines of Black Pine Ridge moving a step on a windless night.

doors.zh: 第三扇，水。一冷——是那一盆洗髓的水；冷过了，化成一条清河。
doors.en: The third, Water. A chill — the marrow-washing basin; then it melts into a clear river.

doors.zh: 第四扇，火。灶膛里的火。娘拨一拨柴：「打不过就跑，跑不丢人。」
doors.en: The fourth, Fire. The fire in the stove. Ma pokes the wood: "If you can't win, run. No shame in running."

doors.zh: 第五扇，土。一股锈味儿，越开越淡——底下，是开春翻开的新土。
doors.en: The fifth, Earth. A smell of rust, fainter as it opens — and underneath, new earth turned in spring.

story.zh:
《落雁三箭》，名字是爷爷听说书听来的，爷爷一辈子没射下过大雁；他爹只教过他头一箭：先看风，后看鹿。练气二层的力气，他头一回全使在一张弓上，那张弓弯得比他爹拉过的哪一回都满，一箭奔面门。邹青松左臂一抬，「当」的一声，箭头撞在他左臂挎着的那面赤铜小盾上，弹了开去；盾面上的火纹，连一道白印也没有。邹青松笑道：「金丹以下，无人能破。」

第二支还没搭上，葫芦塞子已经拔开了，一条火蛇扑了过来。他看的不是蛇，是葫芦嘴：葫芦嘴往哪里偏，蛇便往哪里去。头一扑，他往左一滚；第二扑，往右一跳；第三扑，他跳起来，左边肋下却跟不上——蛇尾正抽在左肋上，「咯」的一声，跟十月十二那夜柴房后头一模一样。火舌舔穿了袄子，舔进皮肉，他横着飞出去，撞在石台上，眼前一白，满嘴的血腥气，左边身子像给人塞进了灶膛。他滚到西北角，那个半人高的黑洞就在手边，他一头钻了进去。

那是一条风道，往下斜，又陡又滑，伸手不见五指。他顺着它往下滚，怀里那只玉匣硌着断了的肋骨。不知滚了多久，身子底下忽然一空，他从一面崖壁半腰的洞口里摔了出去，在黑里落了两三丈，「噗」地落在一样软的东西上。

是个死人。

那是一道干河床——阿禾那张地图上，这里画的是水。秘境里没有天，只有石缝里几处青苔发着一点幽绿的光。他身子底下压着的，是一个本观的灰袍，早凉了，一只手攥着一把短刀，刀口缺了两个牙，另一只手攥成拳，指缝里漏出一点绿。小满趴着没动。他听得见：左边，有一个人在喘，压得极低；前头十来步，有两个，一个在磨牙；右边石头后头，还有一个。四个人，围着河床当中一丛须子又长又硬的细草，都蹲在黑里，谁也不出声，谁也不先动。秘境里黑，人人都是蹲着的猎户。

头顶那个洞口里，有人落了下来，落地极轻。没有火光——邹青松把葫芦塞上了。他也是蹲黑地的人，知道谁先亮，谁先死。

小满攥住了那把短刀，死人的指头硬了，他一根一根掰开。那人在黑里一步一步地找过来，脚步他听得见，那只葫芦他闻得见：一股硫磺味儿，在右前方，不到十步。先看风，后看鹿——黑里看不见风，看不见鹿，只剩下听。小满摸出箭壶里剩下的两支，搭上一支，等脚步停在两步之间，一箭奔那股硫磺味儿去了。

「当」的一声，箭钉在葫芦上，铜塞子崩飞了。火从葫芦嘴里喷了出来，一下子把邹青松照得通亮：一个人，一身黄袍，手里托着一只喷火的葫芦，站在河床正当中。小满捏着嗓子，冲黑地里喊了一声，喊得又尖又怕：「赤松观的！你那葫芦里的宝贝，分我一点——」喊完，他已经滚开了十来步，滚过那丛草，顺手揪了一根。

黑地里蹲着的那四个，听见的是「宝贝」，看见的是一个人、一团火，自己亮在那里。磨牙的那一个先扑了出去，另外三个跟着扑了上去。

那几下，小满没有看全。刀剑砍在那面盾上，「当、当、当」，火星子迸了一地，邹青松还在笑：「金丹以下——」笑声没完，便是火蛇的「嘶嘶」声，一声半截的叫，又一声，跟着是一个人往黑里跑、没跑出十步便倒下的声音。四个人，没有一个喊出第二声。可火光底下，邹青松的左膀子上多了一道剑口子，是从盾沿底下钻进去的，血顺着袖子往下滴，脸白得像纸。他没有走，蹲下去，一个一个摸那四个人的怀，摸出两块灵石、一只银镯子；又一根一根掰开风道底下那个死人的拳头，抠出一撮青苔；那丛草，连根拔了，一样一样揣好，才站起来。

小满已经在崖底下了。他把短刀咬在嘴里，抠着石缝往上爬，断着一根肋骨，爬一尺，眼前白一下。一道缝里，指头抠着一粒圆东西，温的，一跳一跳，他攥住了，塞进怀里。爬到洞口，底下火光一转，一条火蛇贴着崖壁追上来，舔着了他的小腿，裤腿着了火。他滚进风道，把腿往土里一埋，一声没出，手脚并用，往上爬。

他从西北角那个黑洞里滚回石室，没有停，一口气冲出墙缝，冲上了石台。崖壁上那一圈青白的光还亮着，马小宝他们六个人还贴在上头。小满背贴着崖根站住了：困阵粘的是崖壁上的人——那人追出来，只要往崖上蹿一步，便下不来了。

邹青松从墙缝里出来，左膀子垂着，脸上的笑没了，只剩下一层白。他看看小满背后的崖壁，看看崖上贴着的那六个，冷笑了一声：「那阵粘什么，我在石头后头看了一炷香，比你清楚。」他把那面盾往胸前一横，抬起那只喷火的葫芦，「这一回，不跟你玩了。」

葫芦一抖，火出来，分成了四股，四条火蛇，一条从左，一条从右，一条贴着地从正面，一条绕过崖口那片黑，从他背后，一齐扑了上来。背后是崖，崖上是阵；前头是火，脚底下三四步宽，往哪边都是死。崖上有人「啊」地叫了一声。

他使足了浑身的力气，往地上一跺。

脚底板上一烫，像踩着了两块炭。他整个人离了地，离地三尺，贴着地皮横着飞了出去，四条火蛇在他身后撞成一团。他在半空里，落点由不得自己，越过了那汪小潭，「咚」的一声，一屁股坐在了一样又硬又圆的东西上——那只蛫，正趴在墙脚的浅窝里——跟着从壳上滚了下去，滚到它背后。四条火蛇回过头来，追着他扑到，一齐撞在那口「铁锅」上，「嗤」的一声，像四瓢水泼进了灶膛，冒了一阵白烟，灭了。

是可以御火。

邹青松张着嘴，看看灭了的火，看看那只缩了头的蛫，看看缩在龟壳后头的小满，嗓子都劈了：「你这踏马的符是哪来的！？」

小满没有答。他脚底板上那两匹歪马，已经褪得没了影子。

他从包袱里掏出饭桶吐出来的那只木头羊驼——木草泥马——往地上一放。它脖子一伸，认准了主人，撒开四条木腿便追他。小满掉头就跑，绕过小潭，直往邹青松怀里跑。邹青松举盾等着，脚底下却多了一只咔哒咔哒乱撞的木头畜生，绕着他的腿转圈，啃他的靴子。他骂了一声「什么东西」，一脚踢开——

「轰」的一声，木草泥马炸成了一团木屑。小满给掀出去两丈，后背撞在墙上；邹青松倒退三步，黄袍烧穿了半边，眉毛没了，那面盾横在胸前，盾面上连一道白印也没有。

邹青松红了眼。他把空了的葫芦往腰上一掖，举着那面盾扑了上来，盾沿顶住小满的喉咙，把他钉在墙上。小满攥着那把短刀，一刀，一刀，砍在盾面上，火星子一迸一迸，刀口又缺了一个牙，那盾上连一道白印也没有。邹青松喘着气笑：「金丹以下，无人能破。小猎户，你砍你的。」盾沿往里一顶，小满眼前的光一点一点黑下去，耳朵里只剩下水声，一滴，隔很久，又一滴。

胸口的木牌，便在这时烫了。

不是暖，是烫，烫得像一块从灶膛里夹出来的炭。一只半透明的小银狐从他衣襟里钻了出来，蹲在他肩膀上，薄得像一层霜。她眼皮也没抬，从自己那一条尾巴上拔下两根毛，往那面盾上轻轻一甩：「金丹？」

那面盾「咔」的一声，从当中裂开，碎成了七八瓣。两根狐毛余势不减，钉进邹青松的两条腿里，把他整个人掀了出去，撞在崖根的塌石上。他的两条腿往不该弯的地方弯着，瘫在那里，还在喘。那只赤铜葫芦滚到崖沿上，掉进了黑里。

银月在他肩上晃了一晃，又薄了一层，金色的眼睛看着他，什么也没说。

小满扶着墙站起来，咳出两口血。那把短刀还攥在手里。

邹青松瘫在塌石底下，看见他走过来，咧了咧嘴，嘴里冒着血沫子：「……我怀里有灵石。分你一半。」小满没有停。邹青松又道：「赤松观……会来要人的……」小满想起长廊拐角那个胖公子望着长廊顶的眼睛，想起河床上那四个连第二声都没喊出来的人，想起这个人看见过银月。这个人活着出去，石坳村、沉鼎观、他胸口的木牌，一样也藏不住。

他蹲下来。他爹放鹿血，刀从耳根底下进，一拉。他照着做了。

手是干脆的。抖是后来的事。他蹲在那里，手停不下来地抖，耳朵里嗡嗡地响。那一刀下去的手感，那一股热，淌过他的指缝，跟他十二岁那年在溪边，他爹把着他的手给那头鹿放血，一模一样。人跟鹿，原来是一样的。他扭过头去，干呕了几下，什么也没吐出来。

邹青松的怀里，有一只钱袋，鼓鼓的，七块灵石是长廊里那个胖公子的，两块是河床上那几个人的。钱袋底下压着一封信，没封口，字写得歪歪扭扭：**娘：儿在观中甚好。今冬秘境，得了宝便寄钱回去，给小妹置一副嫁妆。**小满看了两遍，把信折好，塞回他怀里。钱袋，他也塞了回去。

「怕了？」肩上那个声音很轻，轻得像要断了。小满没有答。银月道：「怕什么。这一行就是这样，你不杀他，他杀你；你今天放了他，明天死的是你，后天是你娘。」她喘了一口气，「刀，握稳。心，冷一点。」又喘了一口气，「……可你给本王记着，你这把刀，是为什么拿起来的。忘了这个，你就是他。」

话说完，她化作一缕银光钻回了木牌，便没了声息。木牌冰凉，凉得像一块冰；他翻过来看，木牌背面多了一道细细的裂纹，那只蜷着的小狐狸，亮着的那一条尾巴，暗下去了一截。

邹青松腰上挂着名牌。小满解下来看背面：彭城赤松观，邹青松。他在河滩上听执事念过。他拖着他走到石台外沿，那根锈烂的铁橛子跟前，推了下去，又把那块名牌扔了下去。隔了很久很久，底下传上来一声。很轻，像一滴水。

崖上贴着的六个人，一个声音也没有出。

他回到墙里头，把那只玉匣从怀里掏出来，打开。那撮土还在，黄褐色的，松松的，刚好铺满匣底。他想了一想：搁在哪里，都有人来抢。他把它倒在手心里，一口吞了下去。

那撮土一进嘴，便化了，化得像一口温水，滑进丹田，停住了。停了一会儿，它开始**长**。它在他丹田里像一粒种子，「啪」地破开了壳，伸出一根根须子，往他身子的每一个角落里扎去，扎进经脉，扎进骨头，最后，扎进了那五扇门。那五扇门，是他的灵根，又小又乱，像一只漏勺上随手戳出来的五个洞。

须子扎进门缝，往外撑。头一扇是金，「铮」的一声，是爷爷那张弓的弦。第二扇是木，吱吱呀呀，像黑松岭的松树，在没有风的夜里自己往旁边挪了一步。第三扇是水，一冷——是那一夜泡着洗髓的大木盆；冷过了，化成一条清河，一直流到很远的地方去。第四扇是火，暖得他鼻子一酸——是灶膛里的火，他娘拿火钳拨一拨柴：「打不过就跑，跑不丢人。」第五扇是土，最沉，缝里先透出他家后院那股锈味儿，越开越淡，底下透出另一股味道来，香的，像开春头一场雨下透了，一锄头翻开的新土——吴婆婆说过：那时候，这地，是香的。

他跪在石台前头，浑身发抖，涨得像一片刚下过一场透雨的地，只把牙关咬得咯咯地响。等他扶着石台站起身来，走到那面光溜溜的石壁跟前，石壁里照出一个人影，蓬着头，一脸的泥和血——那人影的皮肤底下，有光。金白的，青的，黑的，红的，黄的，五种颜色，一道一道，像五条小河，从心口流到手指尖，又流回来。下下之资，那四个字，是执事拖长了调子念的。换了昨天，他该咧着嘴笑。这时候他只觉得嘴里发苦。

他吸了一口气。石室里的灵气便动了，像一池憋了几百年的水找着了口子，全向他涌了过来。原先五扇漏勺似的小门，吸一口，漏一半；如今五扇大门敞开着，吸一口，进一口——他不是漏勺了，是一口水缸。左边那根肋骨，先是一烫，跟着一麻，再按上去，不疼了；肋下那一片烫焦的皮肉，结了痂。第一天夜里，二层圆满，跟着第三层的关口在他身子里「咯」地一响，像冰面上裂开一道缝。第二天晌午，他冲开了第四层。

竹筒里的水，他全给了那只蛫。头一天夜里，他渴得嗓子冒烟。到后半夜，他听见了一声「叮」。墙角石缝里渗出一道细泉，他趴下去喝了一口，甜得发腻。墙后头有风，风里有潮气；有潮气，就有水。他没算错，只是算早了半夜。

第二天晌午，他把包袱里剩下的那根萝卜啃了。木牌一直是凉的。
story.en:
Felling-Geese Three Arrows: his grandfather had got the name from a storyteller, and never in his life brought down a wild goose; his father had taught him only the first arrow: first read the wind, then the deer. For the first time he put all the strength of layer two into a bow, and it bent fuller than any time his father had ever drawn it; the arrow flew at the face. Zou Qingsong raised his left arm — clang — the arrowhead struck the little red-bronze shield on that arm and glanced off; the flame pattern on its face hadn't so much as a white scratch. Zou Qingsong laughed. "Nothing short of a Golden Core can break it."

Before he could nock the second, the plug was out of the gourd and a fire snake lunged at him. He watched not the snake but the gourd's mouth: wherever the mouth tipped, there the snake went. First lunge, he rolled left; second, he jumped right; third, he leapt, but his left side couldn't keep up — the tail lashed across his left ribs, crack, exactly like that night behind the woodshed on the twelfth of the tenth month. The flame licked through his jacket into the flesh; he flew sideways, struck the altar, his sight went white, his mouth full of the taste of blood, his left side as if stuffed into a firebox. He rolled to the northwest corner; the black hole half a man high was right at his hand, and he dove headfirst into it.

It was a wind shaft, slanting down, steep and slick, pitch dark. He rolled down it, the jade box in his coat grinding against the broken rib. He didn't know how long he rolled; then suddenly there was nothing under him, and he shot out of an opening halfway up a cliff face, fell twenty or thirty feet through the dark, and landed — thump — on something soft.

It was a dead man.

It was a dry riverbed — on A He's map, this was drawn as water. There was no sky in the hidden realm, only a few patches of moss in the cracks giving off a faint green glow. Under him lay one of the abbey's grey robes, long cold, one hand gripping a short knife with two notches in its edge, the other clenched, a little green showing between the fingers. Xiaoman lay still. He could hear: on the left, someone breathing, held very low; a dozen steps ahead, two, one grinding his teeth; behind a rock on the right, one more. Four people, crouched in the dark round a clump of thin grass with long stiff whiskers in the middle of the riverbed, none making a sound, none moving first. It was dark in the hidden realm, and everyone was a hunter crouching.

From the opening overhead someone dropped down, landing very lightly. No firelight — Zou Qingsong had plugged his gourd. He too knew how to crouch in the dark, and knew that whoever lights up first dies first.

Xiaoman took hold of the short knife; the dead man's fingers had gone stiff, and he prised them open one by one. The man came searching through the dark step by step; Xiaoman could hear the steps, and smell the gourd: a whiff of sulphur, ahead and to the right, under ten paces. First read the wind, then the deer — in the dark there was no wind to read, no deer, only hearing. Xiaoman took out the two arrows left in his quiver, nocked one, waited until the footsteps paused between one step and the next, and loosed straight at the smell of sulphur.

Clang — the arrow struck the gourd and the bronze plug flew off. Fire spouted from the gourd's mouth and in an instant lit Zou Qingsong up bright: one man, in an ochre robe, a fire-spouting gourd in his hand, standing in the very middle of the riverbed. Xiaoman pinched his voice and called into the dark, shrill and frightened: "Red Pine! That treasure in your gourd — give me a share —" By the time he'd finished he had rolled a dozen paces away — over the clump, snatching one blade as he went.

The four crouched in the dark heard "treasure", and saw one man, one blaze of fire, lit up there all by himself. The teeth-grinder sprang first, and the other three sprang after him.

Xiaoman didn't see all of what came next. Blades struck the shield — clang, clang, clang — sparks scattering over the ground, and Zou Qingsong was still laughing: "Nothing short of a Golden Core —" Before the laugh was done came the hiss of the fire snake, half a scream, another, and then the sound of a man running into the dark and falling before he'd gone ten steps. Of the four, not one got out a second cry. But in the firelight there was a sword cut in Zou Qingsong's left arm now, gone in under the rim of the shield; blood dripped down his sleeve, and his face was white as paper. He didn't leave. He crouched and went through the four men's coats one by one, came out with two spirit stones and a silver bracelet; then, finger by finger, he prised open the fist of the dead man under the wind shaft and dug out a pinch of moss; the clump of grass he pulled up by the roots; he tucked each away, and only then stood up.

Xiaoman was already at the foot of the cliff. The short knife between his teeth, he climbed by the cracks, a rib broken, his sight going white with every foot. In one crack his fingers closed on something round, warm, beating; he gripped it and stuffed it into his coat. As he reached the opening the firelight below swung round, and a fire snake came up the cliff after him, licked his calf, and his trouser leg caught fire. He rolled into the wind shaft, buried the leg in the dirt, made not a sound, and climbed on, hands and feet.

He tumbled out of the black hole in the northwest corner back into the chamber and didn't stop; in one breath he dashed out through the crack in the wall onto the ledge. The ring of blue-white light on the cliff still shone, and Ma Xiaobao's six were still stuck to it. Xiaoman stood with his back to the foot of the cliff: the binding held whoever was on the cliff face — if the man chasing him took one leap up the rock, he wouldn't come down again.

Zou Qingsong came out of the crack in the wall, his left arm hanging, the smile gone from his face, nothing left on it but white. He looked at the cliff behind Xiaoman, at the six stuck to it, and gave a cold laugh: "What that binding holds — I watched from behind the rocks for a stick of incense. I know it better than you." He set the shield across his chest and raised the fire-spouting gourd. "No more games this time."

The gourd shook, the fire came out and split four ways: four fire snakes, one from the left, one from the right, one low along the ground straight at him, and one curving round over the black of the drop to come at his back — all striking at once. Behind him the cliff, and on the cliff the binding; ahead the fire; under his feet three or four paces of ledge — every way was death. Up on the cliff someone cried out.

He stamped on the ground with all the strength he had.

The soles of his feet burned as if he'd trodden on two coals. His whole body left the ground — three feet off it — and shot sideways skimming the earth, and the four fire snakes crashed into one another behind him. In midair he had no say where he'd land; he sailed over the little pool and — thud — came down seat-first on something hard and round — the gui, lying in the hollow at the foot of the wall — then rolled off its shell and fetched up behind it. The four fire snakes turned and came after him, and all four struck the "iron pot" at once — hiss — like four ladles of water thrown into a firebox; a puff of white smoke, and they were out.

It could ward off fire.

Zou Qingsong stood open-mouthed, looking at the dead fire, at the gui with its head pulled in, at Xiaoman huddled behind the turtle shell, and his voice cracked: "Where the hell did you get that Hoof-It charm!?"

Xiaoman didn't answer. The two crooked horses on his soles had already faded to nothing.

He pulled out of his bundle the wooden alpaca Rice Bucket had spat out — the Grass-Mud Horse — and set it on the ground. It stretched its neck, fixed on its master, and set off after him on four wooden legs. Xiaoman turned and ran, round the little pool, straight into Zou Qingsong's arms. Zou Qingsong waited behind his shield — and found a clattering wooden beast underfoot, circling his legs, gnawing his boots. "What the hell is this," he swore, and kicked it away —

Boom. The Grass-Mud Horse burst into a cloud of splinters. Xiaoman was thrown two zhang and slammed back-first into the wall; Zou Qingsong staggered three steps, half his yellow robe burned through, his eyebrows gone — and the shield across his chest without so much as a white mark.

Zou Qingsong's eyes went red. He jammed the empty gourd into his belt and charged with the shield raised, its rim against Xiaoman's throat, pinning him to the wall. Xiaoman gripped the short knife and hacked at the shield, once, again, sparks spitting, another notch broken from the blade — and the shield hadn't so much as a white scratch. Zou Qingsong laughed, panting: "Nothing short of a Golden Core can break it. Hack away, little hunter." The rim pushed in; the light before Xiaoman's eyes went dark bit by bit, and in his ears there was only the sound of water: one drop, a long pause, another.

Just then the token on his chest grew hot.

Not warm — hot, hot as a coal pulled from a firebox. A half-transparent little silver fox slipped out of his coat and sat on his shoulder, thin as a layer of frost. Without even lifting her eyelids she plucked two hairs from her one tail and flicked them lightly at the shield: "Golden Core?"

With a crack the shield split down the middle and broke into seven or eight pieces. The two fox hairs, their force undiminished, drove into Zou Qingsong's legs and flung him off his feet into the fallen rock at the foot of the cliff. His legs bent where legs don't bend; he lay sprawled there, still breathing. The red-bronze gourd rolled to the edge of the drop and fell into the dark.

Yinyue swayed on his shoulder and grew thinner by another layer; her golden eyes looked at him, and she said nothing.

Xiaoman got up by the wall and coughed up two mouthfuls of blood. The short knife was still in his hand.

Sprawled under the fallen rock, Zou Qingsong saw him coming and bared his teeth in a grin, blood frothing in his mouth: "…There are spirit stones in my coat. Half for you." Xiaoman didn't stop. "The Red Pine Abbey… will come asking for me…" Xiaoman thought of the plump gentleman's eyes round the bend of the corridor, gazing up at the ceiling; of the four in the riverbed who hadn't got out a second cry; of the fact that this man had seen Yinyue. If he walked out alive, Shi'ao Village, Chending Abbey, the token on his chest — not one of them could stay hidden.

He crouched. When his father bled a deer, the knife went in under the ear, and drew across. He did the same.

His hand was clean about it. The shaking came after. He crouched there, his hands shaking and unable to stop, his ears ringing. The feel of that cut going in, that rush of heat running through his fingers — it was exactly the same as the year he was twelve, by the stream, when his father held his hand and they bled that deer. A man and a deer were the same, it turned out. He turned his head away and retched a few times, and brought nothing up.

In Zou Qingsong's coat was a money pouch, bulging: seven stones from the plump gentleman in the corridor, two from the men in the riverbed. Under the pouch lay a letter, unsealed, in a crooked hand: **Mother: your son is well at the abbey. This winter in the hidden realm, when I get treasure I will send money home, to buy little sister a dowry.** Xiaoman read it twice, folded it and put it back in the man's coat. The pouch too, he put back.

"Scared?" The voice on his shoulder was very soft, soft as if about to break. Xiaoman didn't answer. "Scared of what," said Yinyue. "This road is like this: you don't kill him, he kills you; let him go today and tomorrow it's you who dies, the day after your mother." She took a breath. "Hold the knife steady. Keep your heart a little cold." Another breath. "…But you remember this for me: why you took up this knife. Forget that, and you are him."

Having said it, she became a wisp of silver light, slipped back into the token, and fell silent. The token was ice-cold, cold as a lump of ice; he turned it over: on the back was a new hairline crack, and on the little curled fox, the one lit tail had gone dark along part of its length.

A name tablet hung at Zou Qingsong's waist. Xiaoman untied it and read the back: Red Pine Abbey of Pengcheng, Zou Qingsong. He had heard the steward read it out on the flats. He dragged him to the outer edge of the ledge, to the rusted iron spike, and pushed him over, and threw the tablet after him. A long, long while later a sound came up from below. Very faint, like a drop of water.

Of the six stuck to the cliff, not one made a sound.

He went back inside the wall, took the jade box from his coat and opened it. The pinch of earth was still there, yellow-brown, loose, just covering the bottom. He thought a moment: wherever he put it, someone would come to take it. He tipped it into his palm and swallowed it in one gulp.

The moment the earth was in his mouth it melted, like a mouthful of warm water, slid down into his dantian and stopped. It rested a while. Then it began to **grow**. It was like a seed in his dantian: with a pop it split its husk and put out root after root, pushing into every corner of him, into his meridians, his bones, and last of all into the five doors. The five doors were his roots, small and crooked, like five holes poked at random in a skimmer.

The roots pushed into the cracks and prised outward. The first door was Metal: a twang — the string of his grandfather's bow. The second was Wood, creak by creak, like the pines of Black Pine Ridge stepping aside on a windless night. The third was Water, a chill — the big washtub he'd soaked in the night his marrow was washed; past the chill, it melted into a clear river running far away. The fourth was Fire, so warm his nose stung — the fire in the stove, and his mother poking the wood: "If you can't win, run. No shame in running." The fifth was Earth, heaviest of all; through the crack came first the rusty smell of the yard at home, fading as it opened, and under it another smell, fragrant, like new-turned soil after the first soaking rain of spring — Granny Wu had said: back then, this land smelled sweet.

He knelt before the altar shaking all over, swollen like a field after a soaking rain, grinding his teeth till they clacked. When he pulled himself up by the altar and went to the polished wall, it showed a figure, hair wild, face all mud and blood — and under that figure's skin was light. Gold-white, green, black, red, yellow, five colours, stream by stream like five little rivers, from his heart to his fingertips and back. Lowest of the low — four words the steward had drawn out in a long sing-song. Yesterday he'd have grinned. Now there was only a bitter taste in his mouth.

He drew a breath. The qi in the chamber stirred, like water penned for centuries finding a way out, and rushed at him all at once. Before, five little skimmer holes: breathe one, leak half; now five great doors stood open: breathe one, keep one — he was no skimmer now, he was a water vat. The rib on his left went hot, then numb, and when he pressed it, it didn't hurt; the scorched patch of flesh under his ribs scabbed over. The first night, layer two was full, and then the gate of layer three went crack inside him, like ice splitting. At noon of the second day he broke into layer four.

All the water in his flask he'd given to the gui. The first night his throat burned. Past midnight he heard a tink. In the corner a thin spring seeped from a crack; he lay down and drank; it was sickly sweet. There's wind behind the wall, and damp in the wind; where there's damp there's water. He hadn't been wrong, only half a night early.

At noon of the second day he ate the last radish from his bundle. The token stayed cold the whole time.

withdrawn.zh: 火蛇缩回了葫芦，那面盾横在他胸前，他笑眯眯地等着。——再来。
withdrawn.en: The fire snakes draw back into the gourd; the shield across his chest, he waits, smiling. — Again.

exits._grant: 古五: the knife he pried from a dead man's fingers in the dry riverbed (the author, 2026-10-02: 「在秘境中捡一把武器吧」), common iron, 器攻 1.
exits._game: 古五 (2026-10-02): 「九死一生，被追着打」 — a trial he cannot win by force (foe-zou: outlast, his shield is lean hide); the turn is the story's, in this exit's passage: the leap, the 蛫's shell (「是可以禦火」), 银月's two hairs (「金丹？」), and his own knife.
